newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Italian in Indian probe says extradition to fail.
newsitem.headline: Italian in Indian probe says extradition to fail.

text.p: An Italian businessman named in an Indian probe into a $1.3 billion-gun deal involving the Swedish company Bofors AB said he believes any bid by Indian authorities to extradite him will fail.
"I have done nothing wrong and so I am confident this (extradition) will not happen," Monday's New Straits Times newspaper quoted Ottavio Quattrocchi as saying.
Quattrocchi, who lives in Malaysia, was the representative of Italian engineering firm Snamprogetti Spa in New Delhi when India signed the gun deal with Bofors.

Two Indian investigators on Saturday met Interpol officers in the Malaysian capital to seek the extradition of Quattrocchi, who Indian police have linked to suspected payments made by Bofors, the national Bernama news agency reported on Saturday.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday at an Eid al-Fitr celebration hosted by Malaysia's defence minister, Syed Hamid Albar, Quattrocchi reiterated his innocence.
"I think it is unlawful for the Indian government to do this to me," he was quoted as saying by the New Straits Times.

"I am only afraid that it will cause an embarrassment to me and the Italian government to be wrongfully charged like that. I have contacted my lawyer in India and he has assured me that I have nothing to be afraid of," he said.

Officers from India's Central Bureau of Investigation arrived in Malaysia on Friday with warrants for the arrest of Quattrocchi and his wife, Maria, who were among five people named by Indian investigators as recipients of Bofors payments.
Snamprogetti and Quattrocchi on Friday denied any involvement in suspected payments by the Swedish arms maker.

Bernama on Saturday quoted a Malaysian police spokesman as saying that Malaysia did not have an extradition treaty with India. But the court could issue an extradition order if the home minister or his deputy sought it after referring the case to the attorney-general under the Extradition Act 1992.
The uproar over the suspected payments contributed to the 1989 defeat of the government of the late Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, who was accused of involvement in the affair.
Gandhi, who denied the allegations, was assassinated while campaigning for 1991 parliamentary polls.
